logline: A misanthropic, drug-addicted diagnostic genius at a New Jersey hospital solves medical mysteries nobody else can - while running from the one case he cannot crack: himself.

renewal.note: Series concluded May 21, 2012 after eight seasons and 177 episodes on Fox.

bollymeter.basis: The debut season set the procedural template and made Hugh Laurie an American television star. Critics found the show's medical-mystery-as-philosophy format genuinely distinctive: the mystery was always a vehicle for House's worldview, not the other way around.

pull_quotes.text: House M.D. uses the medical procedural format as a delivery mechanism for one of television's great characters.

seasons.review_body: House M.D. Season 1 is a case study in how a great character can carry a procedural format beyond its structural limits. Hugh Laurie's Gregory House, addicted to Vicodin, allergic to social convention, constitutionally incapable of empathy, is one of the great TV character constructions of the 2000s. David Shore understood that the medical cases mattered only insofar as they revealed something about House's worldview, and Season 1 keeps that hierarchy intact. The "Everybody lies" thesis is introduced immediately and dramatised with ingenuity across 22 episodes. The procedural model that follows, built around a brilliant misanthrope, borrows the blueprint Season 1 drew.

episode_reviews.title: Pilot
episode_reviews.spoiler_free: The pilot introduces House in mid-diagnosis - we learn who he is by watching him work rather than through exposition. The patient-of-the-week structure is established, but the show is already signalling that the patient is a lens, not the subject. Laurie's physical performance - the limp, the cane, the painkiller management - is fully developed from the first scene.
episode_reviews.the_moment: House solving the case by making a lateral connection that his team missed - the scene that confirms the show's real subject is the quality of a particular mind, not medicine.

critic_note.text: A pilot that introduces one of television's most compelling characters fully formed.

bollymeter.basis: Season 2 deepened the House-Wilson friendship and delivered 'Three Stories' - the episode frequently cited as the series' single finest hour. Critics considered it the show's first genuine peak.

seasons.review_body: Season 2 is where House M.D. became not just a great procedural but a great character drama. 'Three Stories' (Ep 21) - in which House teaches a medical school seminar using three anonymous cases, one of which is his own - is the show's formal masterstroke and regularly appears on critics' lists of the finest individual episodes in television. The two-part finale featuring Vogler's successor and the shooting arc gave the season genuine dramatic stakes beyond the weekly case. The House-Wilson dynamic was now the show's emotional spine.
seasons.season_over_season: Season 2 is a full creative step up from Season 1 - the show at its most inventive and 'Three Stories' alone makes it essential.

bollymeter.basis: Season 3's Tritter arc - a detective determined to bring House down - gave the show its most sustained antagonist to date; critics were divided on its handling but the season maintained the show's creative momentum.

seasons.review_body: Season 3 introduces Detective Tritter (David Morse) as a multi-episode antagonist targeting House’s drug use, marking a formal departure from the episodic case structure that previously defined the show. The season’s best individual episodes are as strong as anything the series produced, though the Tritter arc’s resolution falls short. The season finale’s team reshuffling is a bold reset that changes the show’s ensemble dynamic for the seasons to come.
seasons.season_over_season: Season 3 is consistent at the show's established standard with a mixed-result season arc - very good without quite reaching Season 2's highs.

bollymeter.basis: Truncated to 16 episodes by the Writers Guild strike, Season 4 introduced a new team-selection format that critics loved, and the two-part finale 'House's Head'/'Wilson's Heart' is universally considered among the show's finest hours.

seasons.review_body: Season 4's team-selection arc, with House holding a competitive process to build a new diagnostic team, delivered a formal reinvention. The shortened season feels dense and purposeful, and the two-part finale delivers the show's most devastating emotional sequence: House in a bus crash, trying to recover a lost memory, while a beloved character faces death. “Wilson's Heart” stands out as the show’s finest episode. The strike's truncation, similar to Lost Season 4, imposed an editorial discipline the series benefited from.
seasons.season_over_season: Season 4 is the show's formal reinvention - and the finale is the series' emotional apex.

bollymeter.basis: 100% on Rotten Tomatoes for Season 5 - critics were unanimous. The season built toward House's psychological collapse and the Mayfield psychiatric hospital finale with the most sustained dramatic arc of the run.

pull_quotes.text: Season 5 represents House at its most dramatically ambitious, with a season arc that pays off more completely than any in the series.

seasons.review_body: Season 5 earned House M.D.'s only perfect Rotten Tomatoes score and stands as the show's most sustained dramatic achievement after Season 4's emotional peak. The season builds methodically toward House's psychological breakdown - the Cuddy relationship, the Kutner death, the Amber hallucinations - culminating in the two-part finale where House voluntarily commits himself to a psychiatric hospital. It is the show's most coherent season-long arc. Critics who had followed the show from the start considered it the series' definitive run.
seasons.season_over_season: Season 5 is the series' creative ceiling - the dramatic arc is the tightest the show ever constructed.

bollymeter.basis: Season 6 opened with a two-hour Mayfield episode that critics praised as among the show's best; the return to Princeton-Plainsboro and the season's back half was considered a partial step down.

seasons.review_body: Season 6's two-hour premiere 'Broken' - set entirely at Mayfield Psychiatric Hospital with a nearly new cast - was praised as one of the finest episodes the show produced. The return to Princeton-Plainsboro with a slightly rebuilt team was a gentle descent from the Season 5 peak. The House-Cuddy relationship finally advancing gave the season's back half forward momentum, and the Wilson-Sam arc provided solid supporting material. A season of strong individual episodes in a slightly lower dramatic register.
seasons.season_over_season: Season 6 is a creative step down from Season 5 - the opener is exceptional, the rest solid but less urgent.

bollymeter.basis: The House-Cuddy relationship season polarised fans - critics found some of it refreshingly different, others found the romance format at odds with the show's character logic. The finale's car-through-house moment divided opinion sharply.

seasons.review_body: Season 7 places House and Cuddy in an actual romantic relationship, handling it with more thoughtfulness than the format demanded but less grace than it needed. The season's first half feels promising, while the second half turns increasingly erratic. The finale, with House driving his car through Cuddy's house, delivers the show's most explicitly melodramatic moment, landing somewhere between operatic and absurd depending on the level of investment. The season ends with House fleeing consequences rather than facing them, setting up the series' last act.
seasons.season_over_season: Season 7 is the show in creative plateau - the romance arc adds something, the finale subtracts credibility.

bollymeter.basis: The final season returned House to prison and then to medicine, and critics gave it measured praise - the finale 'Everybody Dies' was considered a more dignified ending than the show deserved after Season 7's stumbles.

seasons.review_body: Season 8 opened with House in prison, a formal reset that energizes the series and built toward a finale that brings the show’s central relationship to its conclusion. The death of Wilson’s cancer and the final episode’s commitment to that friendship as the show’s real subject ground the story with an honesty it had not reached in years. The finale, though imperfect, feels earned, and it smooths over the friction left by Season 7 stumbles to reach a meaningful conclusion. Eight seasons is a long run, and the final scene holds.
seasons.season_over_season: Season 8 recovers from Season 7's creative lows and finds the right note to end on - not a peak, but a satisfying conclusion.
